Arapaho

Arapaho histories include distinct Northern and Southern community experiences. This reading path connects historical change with particular governments, language education, community-authored research and collaborative public history, keeping regional perspectives separate.

Names & relationshipsNorthern Arapaho Tribe and the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes are separate governments. Cheyenne people are distinct from Arapaho people despite alliance and a shared Oklahoma government; Wind River is shared with the distinct Eastern Shoshone people.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
Adequate initial introduction

Eleven substantive works or conservative collections support an initial educational account of historical change, distinct governments, Northern and Southern educational work, language description, community-authored food research and collaborative public history. Four shorter navigation/overview cards remain supporting. Actual original texts and selected scholarly passages were inspected; older estimates and unread references were excluded. The twelve-source quantity target is not reached. The varied evidence supports continuing alphabetically while retaining explicit limits, not a completion or endorsement claim.

Assessment recorded October 21, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • Historical treaty and removal records, additional Southern community voices and deeper chronological scholarship need further reading. No legal conclusions are drawn from introductory summaries.
  • Selected research and policy texts are not current program evaluations, speaker censuses, complete grammar reviews or permission to reproduce cultural materials.

Start reading here

A short purposeful path through selected actual-content works. Read annotations for community, period and inspection limits; this is not a complete history or community endorsement.

  1. Restorying Northern Arapaho food sovereignty

    Read the situated Northern Arapaho food-sovereignty research as its authors’ historical and qualitative interpretation.

  2. Language and Culture

    Explore the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes’ account of distinct language programs and shared institutions, without merging the two peoples.

  3. Cheyenne and Arapaho Language Apprenticeship Series — Part I and Part II

    Follow the named Arapaho learners’ dated experiences in the selected apprenticeship interviews; aspirations are not measured outcomes.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Northern and southern historical trajectories

The Arapaho Project’s Northern Arapaho history distinguishes northern communities centered on the North Platte from southern communities associated with the Arkansas valley. It places the Northern Arapaho move to Wind River in 1878. Its account also connects boarding schools, allotment and pressures on language with later community-controlled education and cultural renewal. This is a Northern-focused historical synthesis; its undated descriptions of contemporary conditions require fresh corroboration.

Read the sources [6] The Arapaho Project / University of Colorado Boulder

02

Finding the Northern Arapaho government's own resources

The Northern Arapaho Tribe's website identifies Wind River as its location and links governmental and departmental resources. It offers a starting point for a particular tribal government's public information. Its brief homepage is a navigation source; the linked publications require their own reading and dates before supporting detailed historical or policy claims.

Read the sources [12] Northern Arapaho Tribe

03

A shared government's constitutional framework

The Tribes' amended constitution identifies ratification on April 4, 2006. Its preamble links self-government with languages, education and protection of the natural environment. Article II establishes four branches, including the Tribal Council; Articles V–VI distinguish that adult membership body from a legislature representing four Cheyenne and four Arapaho districts. This describes the shared Oklahoma government's framework rather than a constitution for all Arapaho people.

Read the sources [2] Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes, officially linked through Tribal Codes, Acts, and Ordinances

04

Education as an expression of self-determination

The Tribe's 2006 Education Code presents education as part of Northern Arapaho self-determination. It prioritizes Arapaho language, history and culture alongside academic learning and parent and community participation. It expressly disclaims authority over Eastern Shoshone education policy. This dated publication documents the Northern Arapaho government's stated priorities; its presence online does not verify implementation, educational outcomes or unchanged current law.

Read the sources [1] Northern Arapaho Tribe

05

Southern language teaching and public cultural work

The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes describe teaching both distinct languages through community classes, youth outreach, Elder partnerships and an adult apprenticeship program. These are the institution's stated approaches, without a measured fluency outcome. Its Culture Program also describes representatives working on repatriation and with the National Park Service on public interpretation of Sand Creek. These responsibilities concern the shared Oklahoma institution, rather than every Arapaho community's programs or cultural authority.

Read the sources [3] Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes

06

Apprentices describe language learning

In Latoya Lonelodge's 2023 Tribal Tribune interviews, Arapaho apprentice Arianna Long describes progressing from isolated words toward conversation and learning with coworkers while attending college. Rachelle RomanNose discusses pronunciation, expressing herself and the continuing work of learning. Her interest in teaching is an aspiration, not evidence that certification was completed. Their accounts bring individual Southern Arapaho women's voices into a discussion that also includes separately identified Cheyenne learners.

Read the sources [4] Cheyenne & Arapaho Tribal Tribune

07

Approaching Arapaho grammar

The Arapaho Project explains that words can combine many meaningful elements. Verbs can express information that English distributes across several words, including participants, tense and aspect. Its animate/inanimate distinctions are grammatical, rather than a simple division between living and nonliving things. These introductory explanations offer a starting point for exploring language structure; the linked collection should be used with community teaching and does not certify proficiency.

Read the sources [7] The Arapaho Project / University of Colorado Boulder

08

A grammar grounded in documented usage

Cowell and Arapaho coauthor Alonzo Moss, Sr. present their grammar through communicative use as well as forms and rules. Its introduction explains a corpus combining historical records, educational materials and more recent speech, with sources from Wyoming and Oklahoma. The authors identify revisions and corrections to earlier transcriptions. This makes the book useful for understanding how linguistic knowledge is documented, while its evidence remains distinct from a current speaker census.

Read the sources [8] University Press of Colorado

09

Community collaboration in language documentation

Kelly and Cowell describe virtual-reality language documentation developed through iterative work with the Northern Arapaho Language and Culture Commission. Elders helped select contexts, and applications were checked for usability and cultural appropriateness. Sessions in 2019–2020 informed the study. The authors compare elicited language with other documentation methods; their findings concern recorded speech and research design, rather than proof that an application produces fluent learners.

Read the sources [9] Language Documentation and Description; author-deposited version in NSF Public Access Repository

10

Food sovereignty and telling community histories

In a 2019 study, Northern Arapaho researcher Melvin L. Arthur, with Christine M. Porter, relates food sovereignty to community control over historical storytelling. Interviews, talking circles, personal experience and historical research inform his account of disrupted food access and reclamation. He places these changes within colonial dispossession. This is a situated Northern Arapaho interpretation, without demonstrating current clinical outcomes or unanimity among community members.

Read the sources [5] Journal of Agriculture, Food Systems, and Community Development / Lyson Center for Civic Agriculture and Food Systems

11

Descendant knowledge and documentary investigation

The NPS overview describes descendant knowledge alongside archival research in locating and interpreting Sand Creek. Its short orientation provides a starting point for public history, rather than a complete account of the 1864 attack or its aftermath. The linked individual testimony and media were not inspected for this collection.

Read the sources [15] National Park Service

12

Who controls an oral-history project?

Alexa Roberts describes the Northern Arapaho Tribe choosing to conduct its part of the 1999 oral-history project internally. Her account explains why participation and control of research materials mattered, while describing different arrangements with Cheyenne communities. This is evidence about a particular collaborative process. The underlying recordings, interviews and photographs were not accessed or reproduced, and their permissions are not Atlas reuse rights.

Read the sources [11] National Park Service, CRM 23(9); NPSHistory archive reading copy

13

A dated framework for collaborative public history

The December 2017 foundation document identifies tribal histories and consultation as important to interpreting the site. Its planning entries call for further community involvement and review of research. These are dated institutional priorities and identified needs, not proof that proposed projects were completed. They do not establish a single position shared by every Arapaho government or person.

Read the sources [10] National Park Service

14

Directories as access points

The departmental directory lists an Ethete immersion entry alongside other public services. Such listings help readers find Northern Arapaho institutions. A directory alone does not establish current staffing, availability, teaching methods or results. Detailed claims about educational work need a dated publication that explains its purposes, practices and evidence.

Read the sources [13] Northern Arapaho Tribe

15

Finding the Oklahoma government's public institutions

The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes' government overview links its executive, legislative, judicial and Tribal Council branches. This provides an institutional starting point for the shared Oklahoma government; its organization should be kept distinct from Northern Arapaho institutions at Wind River.

Read the sources [14] Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes

What needs further research

  • Read original treaties and additional historical scholarship before making precise territorial, ratification or legal conclusions. Older university wording is not independently verified legal history.
  • Broaden public Southern Arapaho and other community-authored perspectives beyond the shared Oklahoma government and two dated apprentice interviews. Northern and Southern institutions remain distinct.
  • Seek dated educational outcomes and contemporary community priorities without treating an undated program page, a 2006 code or a 2023 interview as current operations or measured success.
  • The grammar and documentation article were inspected in specified selected scopes. No audio was heard, underlying corpus independently reviewed or full grammar read. Public source access is not cultural reuse permission.
  • Sand Creek study methods and park planning contribute to public-history literacy; original recordings, individual narratives, casualty totals and sensitive locations remain outside this account. Community review remains open.

Fifteen cards represent eleven substantive works/collections and four short supporting orientations. Homepage, department directory, shared-government overview and brief NPS stories page stay outside the substantive target. Northern Arapaho and Eastern Shoshone are distinct peoples sharing Wind River. Cheyenne and Arapaho are distinct peoples within the shared Oklahoma government. Neither arrangement establishes one universal authority or identical historical experience. Northern education code enactment is May 4, 2006; the Oklahoma constitution was ratified April 4, 2006 and inspected through a later amended compilation. Neither is asserted to be unchanged current law. Reference grammar authorship includes Alonzo Moss Sr.; selected original introductory content counts once. Online grammar pages form one separate instructional collection, not a count for every lesson link. The 2019 food-sovereignty paper offers situated community-authored interpretation. The 2023 VR paper describes collaborative documentation, not demonstrated learner-fluency gains. Roberts’s 2000 methods paper and the 2017 NPS planning document are distinct works. Original recordings and source media were not accessed, and research permissions do not transfer to Atlas reuse.
